newsitem.title: UK: For East European reformers, foreign money flows.
newsitem.headline: For East European reformers, foreign money flows.

text.p: The countries in Eastern Europe where economic and political reform has not taken root are in turmoil, yet those who have embraced economic change, such as Hungary and Poland, are now seeing tangible benefits.

Hungary, which many commentators thought was on the brink of a Mexico-style financial crisis in 1995, has brought inflation below 20 percent a year, achieved an investment-grade credit rating and seen its stockmarket surge 170 percent in 1996.

"What we have seen is those that have embraced the most effective restructuring, such as Hungary's 1995 austerity plan and Poland's reforms in 1990, reaping the benefits," said Guy Czartoryski, an analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London.

The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, which was set up to aid transition in the region, says productivity growth in Hungary and Poland between 1989 and 1996 was 30-40 percent, in the Czech Republic and Slovakia it has been zero to five percent and in Bulgaria, Albania and Serbia it has been negative.
Openness has been rewarded, Hungary has received some $13 billion of foreign direct investment, Poland $10 billion and the Czech Republic $6.0 billion.
Already this year, foreign investors have propelled Hungary's BUX index of leading shares up more than 1,000 points from its 1996 close of 4,134 points and more is in store.

The market's prospective price earnings ratio for 1997 stands at 11.7 times, compared with 5.9 times at end of 1995, but investors believe that foreign money will continue to flow as relative to their peers in western Europe, Hungarian companies are still cheap and offer greater growth potential.

"In Hungary, you have a stock market which has a similar total capitalisation to Britain's Rentokil and foreign investors simply cannot obtain enough stock," said Tim Harris, head of research at Societe Generale European Emerging Markets (SGEEM).
Major sales include telephone company MATAV, a further tranche of oil company MOL, a stake in drugs company Gedeon Richter, all of which could raise $700 million.
"Hungarian companies are through the restructuring process and are expanding, cermamics maker Zalakeramia intends to make purchases, hotels group Danubius has already done so," said Harris.

In Poland, the structure of the market, of which 40 percent is bank stocks, will be fundamentally altered by the sale of KGHM Polska Miedz SA, Europe's largest copper smelter and that combined with sales of other companies could see $1.0 billion added to stock available to investors.
"New issues increase the profile of these markets and improves liquidity. We have not reached saturation point for foreign investors by any stretch of the imagination," said SGEEM's Harris.

Poland, whose WIG index of leading shares rose 89 percent in local currency terms in 1996, has also seen its bull run continue this year, adding more than 1,500 points to its end-1996 level of 14,342.8.
Consumer price inflation in Poland was 18.5 percent in 1996, down from 21.6 percent in 1995, yet the economy is still growing at five percent plus a year.
"What you are buying in Eastern Europe is growth potential which is extremely cheap, not only in comparison with Western Europe, but also with Latin America and Asia," said Deutsche's Czartoryski.
Merrill Lynch, which has raised exposure to Hungary at the expense of Poland because of the superior earnings potential of the former, believes that reforms bring their own rewards.
"Hungary's performance stands as a beacon for what we expect other countries in the region ultimately to achieve," the U.S. bank said.
